title: Chapter 41 – Hu Wants to Leave
html:
[Lin Clan – Old Hu]

The last thing Hu Tieshou packs is the book.

It lies at the bottom of the third crucible-box in the old granary, under the spare tongs and a bag of fire-clay, wrapped in oiled leather and bound with three turns of copper wire. He has not looked at it in fifteen years. He has not needed to. He knows its weight, its smell, the exact roughness of the bone cover under his thumb. He draws it out in the dark before dawn, with the forge cold and the lamp turned low, and holds it against his chest for a minute like a man holding a sleeping child.

Hundred Veins Forge Canon. Volume One.

It is a thin thing, no thicker than a hand, with covers carved from the shoulder-blade of some great beast and pages of pale vellum written in the cramped, upright script of the Coral Gate. Nine volumes exist, or existed. The other eight burned with the Veiled Forge on a night he does not let himself remember. This one he carried out under his shirt, with one arm, with the blood still running into his sleeve, because it was the only thing in the world he could not bear to leave.

It teaches a man to forge at the Profound grade. It teaches a man to take the heat of a Foundation fire and lay it into steel so that the metal remembers. It teaches, in the margins, in a hand he has not seen in forty years, how to love a thing enough to make it right.

It is also, as far as Hu can tell, the reason that somebody is going to kill him.

He wraps it again. He puts it into the bundle. He ties the knot, and lays his left palm flat on the cold clay of the crucible, once, in farewell. Then he stands, and picks up the pack, and does not look at the anvil.

It is a good anvil. It will stay with the boy.

At the door he stops.

There is a small round thing on the sill, in the gray light, that was not there last night. It is not a stone. It is a pebble in the other sense, round and smooth and the color of old ivory, with a faint pearly sheen. It is sitting very upright, with its head tilted, and its big black eyes fixed on him.

"Not you too," Hu says.

The creature does not blink.

"I have a long road. It would not like you. It would eat you. They eat things like you." He kneels, with a grunt, and sets down the pack. "I have enough trouble. Go back to the boy. He is looking for you."

The pangolin shuffles forward. It puts its nose into the crook of his elbow and begins, with great concentration, to lick the salt from the pocket of his sleeve.

Hu sits back on his heels, and finds, to his considerable surprise, that his eyes are stinging.

"All right," he says. "All right. A little salt."

* * *

It began nine days ago, with a drop of blood.

He found it at the east wall at dawn, on the third stone from the postern, a single dark bead no bigger than a lentil, ringed with three fine red lines. A droplet falling into a pool. The mark of the Blood Shadow's Pool stage. It was fresh. It had been put there in the night, by someone who had walked past three Boundary Alarms and a double guard and left nothing but a smear, and it had been put there for him.

He did not tell anyone. He washed the stone with brine and stood a long time with the bucket in his hand, staring at the water running off it into the dust.

The second sign came three days later. A feather on the granary step, red-brown, a hawk's. It was tied with a thread of black silk. Beneath it, a strip of paper, folded very small, in a hand he had seen on the Veiled Forge's own order books when he was young. Not the Elder's. A clerk's. A scribe.

Two of ours are ash on your slope. We do not ask who. The Elder is not an angry man. He is a patient one. On the ninth day, at the stone cairn where the Salt Road meets the river, there will be a quiet man with a cart. Bring the book. The hill will not be touched.

He read it nine times. He burned it in the forge. And then, because he is an old fool and a coward and the only person alive who knows what the Pool stage does to the families of men who refuse it, he began to pack.

Two of ours are ash.

He does not know who did it. He has a very good idea. He thinks of a boy at a bench with a ruler, and a thin pale line of dried blood on the cuff of his tunic, and a small cold shape that sleeps on his pillow, and his stomach turns over slowly like a dead fish in a pond.

Whoever did it, he thinks, the Elder has decided it was me. A one-armed old artificer with a bent rod. That is what I am for. That is the only mercy anyone has done this house in a year.

If I go, they will believe it.

* * *

He goes out through the east postern at the hour of the hare, in a brown cloak with the hood drawn up, and the Boundary Alarm on the lintel does not so much as warm.

He knows why. He has known since the first night he arrived on this hill. The Patriarch's alarms are set to the Patriarch's blood. A man who walks through them in a hurry, in the dark, with a pack on his back and a face like a closed door, will not be challenged. He will be noticed, in the quiet way of this household, by a hundred small kindnesses that never raise their voices. A guard who looks away. A cook who leaves a bundle of rice cakes on the gate-seat, wrapped in a dry cloth. A stable boy who has put a mule outside the wall, saddled, and gone to bed.

Hu sees the mule. He stands still in the frost-gray light and looks at it for a very long time.

"Ah," he says, very quietly, to nobody. "You are all fools."

He goes past it. It is easier to walk.

The track leads north, along the line of the wall, then down through a stand of young pines to the old quarry road. It is a rough way, rutted and iced. He knows it blind. He has walked it every night for a year, to the spoil heaps and back, with a jar of wine and a head full of the one thing he has never been able to forget. Forty steps down, and nobody to ask. A door at the bottom, and no key.

He is two hundred paces from the wall when he becomes aware that the pines have stopped dripping.

It is a small thing. A hush. A stillness in the cold air, as though a hand had been laid across the mouth of the forest. His good arm goes to his belt before he has thought.

"I do not think you should go that way," says a voice.

Lin Wenyuan sits on a fallen log at the edge of the road, in a plain brown robe, with his left hand folded over his right and a lantern at his feet. He does not seem to have been waiting. He seems to have been sitting there, in the cold, for a long time, thinking about something else.

Hu stops. He does not turn his head. "Patriarch."

"Old Hu." The lantern's light makes a small gold room around them. "Sit down, please. It is a long walk to the river, and I have something to say."

"I would rather walk."

"I know. That is why I have been sitting here since the fourth watch." A very faint, dry note. "I thought you might like the company."

* * *

They are not alone.

Hu sees it as he sits. He has been walking with his head down, listening to the thing in his chest, and has not been looking. But there are shapes in the pines now, quiet, patient, at the edges of the lantern's reach. Su Qinghe leans against a trunk ten paces off with her gardener's hat in her hand and her knife loose at her back. She does not look at him. She looks at the road.

And on the stump of an old oak by the track, a small, gray-clad figure sits with his knees drawn up and a pale scaled shape curled at his ankle. A boy of ten. He has his hands in his sleeves. His face in the lantern light is white and perfectly composed, and his eyes are very large.

"You told them," Hu says to the pangolin, without heat.

Pebble, with great dignity, looks away.

"It was not the pangolin," Jian says. "It was the wall. Father's alarm warmed when you took the rice cakes. I heard it from the other side of the house." A pause. "I did not want you to walk the whole road alone, and I did not want you to have to say goodbye to me."

Hu does not trust his voice. He sets down the pack.

"Patriarch," he says finally. "I have to tell you what I am carrying."

"I know what you are carrying."

"Do you?"

"A book." Wenyuan's tired eyes rest on him. "A forging manual. A very old one, in a language of metal and fire. One of nine, the others lost. A sect in the south has wanted it for fifteen years. I am a talisman drawer, Old Hu, not a fool. I do not know what it says. I know what it is worth."

Hu closes his eyes.

"It is not the book," he says. "Not only. It is what the Elder wants it for. He has the Veiled Forge's records. He has the guild's list of apprentices. He knows that I was the last journeyman of the line, and that the Canon was not meant to be read by one man. It was meant to be a key." His voice is very low. "Nine volumes. One for each stage of a great formation. A forge that makes a forge. I only ever read the first. I do not know what the rest were for. But I know that a man like the Elder does not hunt for fifteen years, and send rogues, and risk his scouts, for a book that merely teaches a man to forge steel."

"A key to what?"

"I do not know." Hu opens his eyes. "I have been trying to guess. I am afraid to guess."

Nobody speaks. The lantern hisses softly.

"So," Wenyuan says. "You intend to go to the Salt Road and give it to them."

"I intend to give them me." The words come out harder than he means. "That is what the note says. Bring the book. Bring yourself. The hill will not be touched. Do you think they would stop at me, Patriarch? Do you think a man like Mu would bargain for a book and leave a granary full of ingots and a family full of talismans standing behind it?"

He stops.

He has said the name. It is out in the cold air between them, and nothing he can do will put it back.

"Mu," says Su Qinghe, very softly, from the trees.

"I did not mean—"

"You said Mu."

"It was in the clerk's script." He puts his hand over his eyes. "The paper was sealed with an Elder's cipher. Pool stage. I know the cipher. I have known it for twenty years. There were only ever three living men who used it, and one of them taught me to forge a blade." His voice cracks, very slightly. "I did not want to say it. If I say it, it is real."

"It was already real," Wenyuan says.

* * *

It is Jian who speaks next.

He has been silent through all of it, a small still shape on a stump, with the pangolin pressed against his ankle. He does not lift his voice. He does not stand. He says, in the careful, plain tone of a child reading a lesson, "Old Hu. May I ask you something?"

"Ask."

"If you go to the Salt Road, what happens at the end of the day?"

"I give them the book."

"And then?"

"They take me."

"And then?" The boy's eyes do not leave his face. "They have a patient Elder. They have a cart. They have a very large amount of time. You are the last journeyman of a line they have been hunting for fifteen years. What do they do?"

Hu says nothing.

"I think they do not kill you," Jian says. "Not first. I think they keep you. For a long time. They make you read the book aloud, and write down what you remember of the other eight. They put you in a room with a forge and a fire, and they tell you that the hill is safe so long as you keep working." His voice is quite steady. "And then one day they stop telling you."

The cold air presses on Hu's ears.

"You have thought about it," he says slowly.

"For nine days. Since the feather." The boy's mouth tightens, once. "I found it first. On the step. I put it back. I thought you would want to be the one who decided."

"You—"

"I did not want to take it from you. But I could not let you walk the road without telling you what I think." He draws a breath. "Hu. You told me once that you wanted to see what happens next. You said it standing at the forge, with the hammer in your hand. I thought it was the first thing you had said in a year that sounded like you meant to stay."

Hu stares at him.

"I did," he says. His voice is a rasp. "Heaven help me. I did."

"Then it is simple." Jian's hands unclench in his sleeves. "A trap needs the bait to stay in the room."

There is a stillness. Then, from the pines, very softly, Su Qinghe laughs.

It is a short, rueful, broken sound, almost a cough. She straightens from the tree, and crosses the road, and stands at her son's shoulder with her hat pressed to her chest. "He is right," she says. "He is irritatingly right. You cannot be the bait on the Salt Road, Hu. You would be the bait in a cage, in a house we cannot find. You must be the bait here, on a hill we know, behind a wall we have been building for a year, with a dozen pins in the ground and a woman who has done this before." She meets his eyes. "Stay. Let them come to us."

"They will come with a Foundation elder."

"Then we will see what he is worth."

"Su Qinghe, you are a Qi Refining fourth-stage with a good knife."

"And you are a one-armed man with a bent rod and a boy who counts." Her eyes glitter. "I am aware of what we have."

Hu looks at the three of them. A Patriarch on a log. A woman in a hat. A child on a stump. And the pangolin at the child's ankle, which has stopped licking the salt and is looking up at him with grave black eyes, in a perfect imitation of someone who has been listening.

He thinks of a long road to a river and a quiet man with a cart.

He puts his face in his good hand and begins, to his deep and abiding disgust, to laugh.

* * *

"We cannot hold the hill against a Foundation elder," Hu says, an hour later, in the granary, with the lamp lit and the pack on the bench and the whole family sitting around him on crates and buckets in the gray light. "I want that said. I have been saying it for nine days to the inside of my own skull and I would like it said out loud."

"It is said," Wenyuan replies. He holds a cup of hot tea in both hands. "Go on."

"Elder Mu is Pool stage. Not the least of them. I would say mid, from the cipher. He has a Foundation fire, and a Foundation sense, and he carries a bone drum." Hu rubs his face. "I have met drummers. They stun. A man hears the beat and his channels lock. It does not last long. But a few breaths is all they need."

"A drum." Jian's eyes go distant. "How far does it carry?"

"A hundred paces, in the open. Less in a wood. A stunned man is a dead man." Hu pauses. "Not that Mu would use it himself. He would send a drummer ahead. A Drip. They are always Drips, QR nine, with a bone drum and a bad temper."

"We can plan for a drum."

"We can plan for this drum, because I have just told you. I do not know what else he has. That is the trouble." Hu spreads his hand on the bench. "I know the Pool, Patriarch. I do not know Mu."

"Then we find out what Mu is." Wenyuan sets down the cup. "The Salt Road is a Sect road. If Blood Shadow enters it with a cart and a hunter, the Hall has the right to know. I will write to the Arbiter this morning. Not about you. About the road."

"The Hall will do nothing."

"The Hall will write it down. That is all I need." The Patriarch's voice is dry. "A thing that is written down can be cited later. I am my father's son, Old Hu. I know how to build a paper wall."

Hu stares at him.

"And the second thing," Wenyuan goes on. "My brother Wenshi's guards escort a caravan on that road, every second week. I will pull them. If your elder wants a cart at a cairn, he will find nobody there but a stone."

"He will find a note," says Jian.

They look at him.

"A note." The boy's face is quite grave. "From the Patriarch. A courteous one. I regret that the guest elder is unwell and cannot attend. His book is not for sale. The Hill of Green Pine sends its regards. Signed, and sealed, and left under the cairn." He thinks. "It tells him three things. That we have understood him. That we are not afraid. That we have not given him anything."

"It tells him we are angry." Hu is almost laughing again. "You want to insult a Pool elder."

"I want him to have to decide." Jian shrugs. "A patient man is dangerous because he waits. If he has to answer a letter, he cannot."

Mother makes a sound like a swallowed cough. Wenyuan puts his hand over his mouth. Pebble, on the bench, has begun, very slowly, to lick the lamp-oil from the base of the wick.

"Stop that," Jian says absently.

No. A tiny, stubborn, wordless feeling passes between them. Hu sees the boy flinch, very slightly, and understand.

"It says salt," Jian murmurs. "It says the oil is salty."

"It is salty," says Hu. "It is whale oil."

"Then it is not for eating."

Yes. Yes. Salt.

"No."

They all stare. The boy has the expression of a child holding off a puppy with great gravity. The pangolin's tail has curled up over its back, in an unmistakable attitude of insult.

Wenyuan begins, quietly and helplessly, to shake.

It is the first time Hu has seen the Patriarch of Green Pine Hill laugh. It takes him a long time to stop.

* * *

That evening, when the others have gone to their rooms and the granary is full of the slow warm quiet of a banked fire, Jian comes back alone.

He is carrying a Light Orb slip and a small wooden stool. He sets the stool beside the anvil and sits, with the pangolin in his lap, and does not say anything for a while. The orb makes a circle of pale gold on the floor.

"I would like to try something," he says at last. "With Pebble. The great ring is rebuilt. Twelve pins around the stone hut, six plates under the road. I have been trying to find out what it will do against a seam."

"A seam."

"It is the word it uses. I do not know if it is the right one." He turns the pangolin over in his hands, gently, so that its pale belly shows. "It looks at barriers and finds the place where two parts meet. It has done it with Qi shells. With the Mirror Guard. With a pit-trap. I think a ring may be the same."

"You want to put the pangolin in the ring?"

"I want it to walk through."

Hu does not say no. He has learned, over the past three days, that the question is rarely whether, with this child. It is how soon. He rises, with his knee cracking, and takes the lamp from its hook.

They go out together under the stars.

It is a mild night, with the first soft smell of spring on the wind. The ring lies in the dark on the hill above the stone hut, a great circle of black iron posts driven into the ground and wired together with spirit copper. Hu rebuilt it himself, one pin a dawn, for ten months. He knows every post. When he lays his hand on the nearest, the whole structure answers him, a long, deep, silent hum, like the breath of a sleeping animal.

Jian sets the pangolin down in the grass, ten paces outside the ring. He crouches beside it. He puts a hand on its back, and says something too soft to hear.

Pebble does not move for a long time.

Then it lifts its head, and tilts it, and walks forward across the grass in the slow, rolling, deliberate gait of a creature that has all the time in the world. It reaches the circle. It stops at the base of the fourth pin. It sniffs, once. And then, without hurry, without any sign of effort, it steps through it.

Hu feels it. It is not a sound. It is a sensation in his bones, a faint, dry, delicate give, as if somebody had drawn a thumbnail across the stretched skin of a drum. The ring holds. Every pin sings its note. But in the space between the fourth and fifth posts, a thing the width of a hand has gone silent.

A gap. A seam. A place where the weaving does not quite meet.

The pangolin trots out of the ring on the far side, shakes itself, and sits down in the grass to wash its face.

Nobody says anything for a long time.

"I laid that ring," Hu says. His voice does not sound like his own. "I laid it. Every pin. I tested every field with a mirror and a stone. There is no gap."

"There is," says Jian. "I have scanned it four times. There is nothing there. It is not a fault. It is where the structure meets itself." The boy's face is white in the lamp. "It only found it because it is looking for places like that."

"A ring is a closed circuit—"

"A closed circuit still has to close somewhere." He looks up. "Hu. If it can find a seam in a ring you built, it can find a seam in anything."

A cold wind moves across the hill. The pins hum.

Hu thinks of a man with a cart at a river cairn, and a drum, and a patient Pool elder who has hunted the last journeyman of the Coral Gate for fifteen years and sent his scouts, twice, to find a creature the size of a loaf of bread. He thinks of nine volumes of a manual that was meant to be a key. He thinks of the word key.

The refiner to make the lock. The seamwalker to open the door.

It is not a thought he has ever had before. It comes to him whole, like a stone dropping into a well, and it goes down a very long way.

"Jian," he says slowly.

"Yes?"

"I think I know what he wants it for."

The boy waits.

"I do not know where." Hu turns, and looks back at the dark shape of the hill, the roofs, the wall, the black stone hut at the head of the quarry road. "But I think I know what kind of place it is. And I think it is a very great deal closer than the Salt Road."

On the wall of the east tower, a single bell begins to ring.

It is the night watch, calling the hour. Hu has heard it ten thousand times. But tonight it falls in the dark like a stone into black water, and he stands with his hand on the humming iron, and listens to it, and does not move until the last note has died away.
